item.title: Meek Mill Says He’ll Quit Rap If His New York Concert Plan Proves Him Wrong
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Meek Mill puts his rap career and REFORM role on the line as he vows to fund and book his own New York show before 2027.
item.content:encoded:
Meek Mill says he’ll quit rap if his plan to put on his own New York concert proves him wrong.

His wager follows a fight with Live Nation over where he can perform, who can book him and how the company promotes his shows.

“Nyc will be my next show ima book and run it let’s see the difference if im wrong i will quit rap and step down from reform … im willing to bet my legacy on it! This is in play now!!!! Before 2027 too! It’s really that easy,” Meek wrote on X.

Meek said the first stop after Philadelphia should’ve been New York, not Los Angeles.

“I would of went from philly to nyc not la first that dosent make any sense even with production … ima do it with my own money and production before January first! To give a example of what’s been happening to me! Nyc my next show!!!!!!!!!!” he wrote in a separate post.

The Dream Chasers Nights run opened November 24 in Philadelphia, but New York wasn’t on the original itinerary.

Ticketmaster lists all five remaining dates as canceled: Los Angeles at the Hollywood Palladium on November 29, Boston at MGM Music Hall at Fenway on December 5, Baltimore at CFG Bank Arena on December 11, Chicago at the Aragon Ballroom on December 18 and Atlanta at the Coca-Cola Roxy on December 20.

Meek said his exclusive deal kept him from taking offers from other promoters while Live Nation controlled the routing and gave him dates he didn’t want.

He also questioned whether the company had done enough to sell tickets in Los Angeles, asking people to show him a billboard after he said he’d been told the show was advertised.

The ticket notice didn’t give a reason for the cancellation.

Meek helped start REFORM Alliance in 2019 after his imprisonment, and the probation and parole advocacy group lists him as a co-chair.

Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino sits on its board.

Meek said in a separate X post Friday that he wasn’t feuding with Rapino personally and was taking issue with the system he says has held him back.

item.title: Nicki Minaj Calls Elon Musk A ‘Hero’ Over SpaceX Stock Pledge For Children
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Nicki Minaj called Elon Musk a hero after he said he and SpaceX would give children shares through Trump Accounts.
item.content:encoded:
Nicki Minaj called Elon Musk a “Hero” after he said he and SpaceX would give two shares of the company to children in the United States.

The rapper offered the one-word endorsement in a November 27 post on X that shared Musk’s announcement about the stock pledge.

“Every child in America will receive two SpaceX shares, one from the company and one from me personally,” Musk wrote.

His post described the gift broadly, but the company’s announcement laid out a specific way it intends to get the shares to children: through existing Trump Accounts.

In its November 25 announcement, SpaceX said it would put one newly issued share of Class A common stock into every “currently active Trump Account.”

SpaceX said Musk would personally match the number it gives. Musk said he expects SpaceX’s shares to transfer in December and his own to transfer after a restriction on his stock expires in June 2027.

The company described both contributions as commitments, not completed transfers, and noted the plan was subject to uncertainties including third-party and government approvals.

The shares aren’t the same as the government’s $1,000 deposit.

The IRS describes Trump Accounts as investment accounts for children. The federal pilot contribution has a narrower eligibility window: U.S. citizens born from January 1, 2025, through December 31, 2028, with valid Social Security numbers. Families must claim the deposit separately. SpaceX’s statement refers to currently active accounts rather than just children who qualify for that federal payment.

Minaj had backed the account program before Musk announced the match.

In January, AllHipHop reported that she pledged between $150,000 and $300,000 to help fund accounts for newborns of her fans.

In an X post announcing her involvement, Minaj gave her reason for backing the program: “Early financial literacy & financial support for our children will give them a major head start in life.”

Minaj had praised Musk in person, too. During a May visit to SpaceX’s Starbase, she appeared on the company’s webcast in a Starship T-shirt that nodded to her 2012 single “Starships.” Speaking on the webcast before a technical issue forced SpaceX to scrub the launch attempt, she told him, “Elon, thank you for everything that you’re doing for humanity.”

item.title: BFG Baandz Killing: Dallas Police Release Images Of Two Suspects
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Dallas police release surveillance stills and ask for help identifying two suspects in the August killing of BFG Baandz.
item.content:encoded:
BFG Baandz’s killing has Dallas investigators looking to the public to identify two people captured on surveillance footage.

The Dallas Police Department released images on November 25 and described a silver Ford Mustang with a blue racing stripe as a clue in the August shooting.

Detective Joshua Romero told FOX 4 Dallas-Fort Worth that he wants to hear from anyone who recognizes the people in the images or remembers seeing the car.

Romero acknowledged that the distance could make the people hard to recognize and urged anyone with information about who might have wanted to harm the rapper to come forward.

“Somebody knows something, and that’s what I’m looking for,” Romero said.

The new appeal follows a shooting outside a gas station in the Pleasant Grove neighborhood of southeast Dallas.

Officers answered a call in the 100 block of North Jim Miller Road at about 3:20 A.M. on August 27, and Dallas Fire-Rescue took the rapper to the hospital in critical condition.

The Dallas County Medical Examiner’s Office recorded his death at Baylor University Medical Center at 8:30 A.M., about five hours after the call, and ruled it a homicide.

Dallas Police identified the 24-year-old victim the next day.

“He’s been a staple in this community,” Romero said of BFG Baandz, who put out the eight-track project Snowed In in February, with a track named for former Dallas Mavericks star Dirk Nowitzki.

He also produced “New Dallas Symphony,” a March release from Real 4 Baby that brought together six guests, including Montana 700, BigHomie Kevi and Hustleman Quise.

item.title: Tulisa Takes On Britain’s Tabloids After The Drug Case That Fell Apart
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Tulisa revisits a tabloid sting in a new Paramount+ series and calls for an independent regulator to hold the press to account.
item.content:encoded:
Tulisa wants Britain to change who polices its newspapers after a tabloid sting put her on trial. The N-Dubz member revisits the cocaine case that collapsed without a conviction in Tulisa: The Reckoning, a three-part series premiering November 26 on Paramount+ in the United Kingdom and Ireland.

The case still follows Tulisa years after she walked out of court. “To this day, people still think I was done for drugs,” Tulisa told Radio Times. The series follows the British Hip-Hop and R&B performer from her rise alongside Dappy and Fazer to her turn as a judge on The X Factor.

The criminal charge stemmed from a 2013 operation by The Sun on Sunday reporter Mazher Mahmood, who posed as a film producer. Tulisa was accused of arranging a cocaine deal for him and denied the charge. A judge halted her trial in July 2014 after finding strong grounds to believe Mahmood had lied in court.

The witness statement at the center of that decision later led to a trial of Mahmood and his driver, Alan Smith. A judge said Smith had changed his account to remove information that could have helped Tulisa argue she’d been entrapped.

A jury convicted both men in 2016 of conspiring to interfere with justice, and Mahmood received 15 months in prison while Smith received a suspended 12-month sentence.

Tulisa now wants a regulator that newspapers can’t fund, appoint or control, with the power to investigate complaints and impose fines.

Her Fix the Press petition asks the government to act on recommendations from the Leveson inquiry into press practices. Tulisa told The Upcoming, “This is why I’m doing it to protect other people from having it happen to them again and again and again.”

Labour lawmaker Josh Newbury is scheduled to lead a Westminster Hall debate on independent press regulation on December 10.

item.title: Justin Timberlake Tells Jimmy Fallon Why He Opened Up For Apple TV Documentary
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Justin Timberlake tells Jimmy Fallon how a director he trusted got him to discuss parts of his life he'd kept private.
item.content:encoded:
Justin Timberlake put things in his Apple TV documentary that he says he’d never even shared with some of the people closest to him.

He told Jimmy Fallon he hadn’t planned to make a documentary about himself until a series of conversations with director Fisher Stevens changed his mind.

Stevens already knew Timberlake from directing him in the 2021 Apple film Palmer, but Timberlake said that relationship didn’t give him an automatic yes.

“I’m sort of famously private,” he explained in an interview on The Tonight Show. Their conversations eventually got him interested in telling stories beyond the ones people could piece together from the headlines.

Timberlake told Fallon that opening up for Stevens meant revisiting experiences from the past five years that changed the way he saw himself as a husband, father and friend.

“I found the whole experience to be really cathartic,” Timberlake said after telling Fallon he had to work up the nerve to go through with it.

He hopes that talking about his life gives people dealing with their own troubles a reason to talk about what they’re going through, too.

The subjects Timberlake was willing to discuss with Stevens go beyond what he was ready to spell out on the couch.

He didn’t name the private stories he put on camera, though Apple’s trailer for the four-part series revisits his 2004 Super Bowl appearance with Janet Jackson, his relationship with Britney Spears, and the arrest that led to a 2024 guilty plea on a reduced impaired-driving charge.

The career footage also puts Timberlake back alongside producers Pharrell Williams and Timbaland, and the Fallon appearance gave him a chance to talk about writing songs for FutureSex/LoveSounds on its 20th anniversary.

Timberlake performed selections from the album on the show, including “My Love,” the T.I. collaboration that won a Grammy for Best Rap/Sung Collaboration.

Fallon and Timberlake also turned their old “History of Rap” routine into a medley of party songs, this time singing the Backstreet Boys hit “I Want It That Way.”

Apple TV will release the first two episodes on December 11, followed by the third on December 18 and the finale on December 23.

item.title: Ginuwine Goes After His Masters In New My Ride Browser Game
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Ginuwine stars in a free story game that sends players into a fictional Sony Music office to reclaim his master recordings.
item.content:encoded:
Ginuwine pulls up outside a record company in the rain and asks players to help him get his music back. That’s the opening of MY RIDE: The Ginuwine Story Game, a free browser game that turns ownership of master recordings into the objective of a fictional mission.

Ginuwine told fans on Instagram why he wanted them playing: “the premise is to get my masters back from my label and live free and get what’s owed to me after over 30 years.”

He had described what that meant long before the game. Ginuwine told YouKnowIGotSoul he would record 25 to 30 songs for a 12-track album. Because he didn’t own the recordings, the label kept even the songs it left off. He estimated Sony still had 100 of his songs. The game lets fans play out his wish to reclaim them; his announcement described no lawsuit or deal to bring them home.

“Look at that tower. Every light on in there… my records paid for half of ’em,” the character says in the game’s dialogue. The scene then hands control to the player outside the building, with a guard near the entrance and a first objective that sends you inside.

The controls let players move, sneak, dodge, punch and kick, and a separate action button handles interactions.

Ginuwine stars in the game, but the title screen and credits identify LMG as its creator and credit him with design and direction.

The game brings in Timbaland, Missy Elliott, Tank, Tweet and Aaliyah under its Supafriendz banner. Those credits describe the lineup of characters and don’t establish that the artists recorded dialogue or helped build the game.

The game sends its lead toward a fictional Sony office, but the company connection goes back to Ginuwine’s first record.

Epic, a division of Sony Music, released “Pony” through 550 Music, with Timbaland producing the track and Ginuwine and Static Major among its writers.

Recording engineer Jimmy Douglass recalled taking a two-track recording of the song to Sony before the company signed Ginuwine and Timbaland.

While My Ride spins that label history into a fictional mission, Ginuwine has also been working with his son on a book about his own life.

item.title: Mariah Carey’s Christmas Classic Becomes A Sesame Street Lesson
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Mariah Carey's holiday anthem gets a Muppet makeover as Elmo and friends work the letter U into Christmas morning.
item.content:encoded:
Mariah Carey has a new set of singers putting her Christmas song to work as a vocabulary lesson.

Sesame Street’s Abby Cadabby, Elmo, Grover and Cookie Monster turned “All I Want for Christmas Is You” into an ode to the letter U, complete with a green U in a Santa hat bouncing along.

The Muppets use Christmas morning to show what would be harder to say if the letter went missing, from undoing ribbons to dealing with a knot of string lights.

In the video Sesame Street shared, Grover wants a ukulele, Abby asks for a unicorn, and Elmo has his eye on a UFO. Cookie Monster saves his guess for after the music, pulling a pair of heart-print underwear out of a box.

“It’s a letter U Christmas miracle!” Cookie Monster says as he holds up the gift.

Elmo, Abby and Cookie Monster already shared a song in the season premiere, which arrived November 23 on Netflix and PBS Kids.

Zara Larsson joined the trio for “Puppy Dance Party” in an episode where Grover helps track down a lost present for Tango’s cousin.

This season also uses its stories to help children practice sharing, listening and working out disagreements. The show had already used another pop hit to teach teamwork, adapting “Golden” from KPop Demon Hunters for an August video.

Carey’s original drew on her own childhood, when Christmas gave her something to look forward to even when family gatherings didn’t go the way she hoped.

“I wanted it to make people happy and make myself happy,” Carey told the Library of Congress in an interview for the National Recording Registry.

She brought the melody and lyrics she had started at the piano to co-writer Walter Afanasieff, and the recording appeared on her 1994 album Merry Christmas. The holiday single became her first recording inducted into the National Recording Registry in 2023.

The original remains part of Carey’s own holiday shows, including a recent performance in Rio de Janeiro where she also sang “Oh Santa!” and “We Belong Together.”

Her U.K. run begins Friday at Birmingham’s Utilita Arena before moving to London’s O2 on November 30.

Carey closes the three-date U.K. leg at Manchester’s Co-op Live on December 2.

item.title: Too $hort Explains Why He Passed On A Trump-Linked Appearance
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Too $hort draws a line between voter registration shows and a political invitation he felt would signal support for Trump.
item.content:encoded:
Too $hort turned down a political appearance because he thought getting onstage would look like an endorsement of Donald Trump.

The Oakland rapper said in an interview on Flagrant and Funny that the invitation came from a Trump supporter, not directly from someone in the president’s circle.

Too $hort told hosts Cari Champion and Jemele Hill that he saw the event as political even without a phone call from Trump’s team.

“I don’t want to align myself with that because it’s just something that I wasn’t supporting,” Too $hort said. He didn’t name the person who approached him or identify the event.

That’s different from how Too $hort described the voter registration concerts he has done through Democratic organizers.

He said the shows were free to the public, with registration part of getting in, but nobody was told whom to vote for.

He remembered being offered twice his usual fee for a Milwaukee appearance and drew a line between getting people to register and letting an appearance stand as support for a candidate.

Too $hort didn’t describe the Trump-linked invitation as a million-dollar offer, either.

The interview turned to whether someone might reconsider if offered $1 million for two appearances, and he said he hadn’t faced that choice.

Too $hort has pushed back before when his name was used to suggest he backed Trump.

In 2020, he publicly rejected how a documentary grouped him with Trump supporters and said at the time that he had passed on a separate effort to get him to travel to Washington to meet with the president.

In the new interview, he focused on how somebody can read a political message into an artist simply taking the stage.

The conversation about political invitations followed a question about former Vice President Kamala Harris. Too $hort said the two move in some of the same circles but pushed back on the suggestion that they’d previously bumped into each other.

Asked about Kamala Harris being a Too $hort listener, the rapper joked that he would’ve pegged her as more of an MC Hammer fan.

item.title: Ja Rule Considers Giving His Album An AI-Generated 70s Makeover
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Ja Rule hears a familiar hit recast in a different era and weighs bringing that sound to an entire album from his catalog.
item.content:encoded:
Ja Rule heard artificial intelligence turn “Put It On Me” into a record that sounded like it came out in the 1970s, and now he’s considering giving a whole album the same treatment.

“I’m thinking about repurposing like one of my whole albums like that and just put it out as a ’70s vibe,” Ja Rule said in a Yahoo Finance interview.

He described the reworked single in four words: “It sounded fucking amazing.”

The song that caught his attention is from Rule 3:36, his second album, released in 2000.

The original album recording features Vita, and the version credited on Billboard’s Hot 100 with Lil’ Mo and Vita reached No. 8 in March 2001. Tru Stylze and Irv Gotti are credited as producers on the album recording.

The original song earned Ja Rule and Vita a Grammy nomination for Best Rap Performance by a Duo or Group.

Ja Rule also said he’d consider using the technology before a song is recorded, not just after it’s out.

When he writes for other singers, he said he has used a vocalist to record a guide so they can hear how the song is meant to go. He said a generated voice could do that job instead, or potentially stay on a song he wrote if he liked the result.

“Now I don’t have to do that if I don’t want. I could write this record, you know, feed it to the AI model, let it sing it and then send it to the artist. Or actually say, wow, this sounds amazing with the AI voice. Maybe I’ll leave it and put it out as an AI song,” Ja Rule said.

Ja Rule’s interest in making another version of an older album comes after he’d discussed a possible sale of his catalog in 2023.

At the time, he said he’d want a deal that let his family buy back a share later. In talking to Sozzi about the music now, Ja Rule described streaming as a source of checks he wasn’t getting a decade ago.

Ja Rule told Sozzi that nobody had approached him to make AI music when the host asked whether he’d been pitched a project.

item.title: Jay-Z Reveals Muhammad Ali Wanted To Punch Him In The Face
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Jay-Z laughs about his run-ins with Muhammad Ali and explains what sold him on the actor playing his childhood hero.
item.content:encoded:
Jay-Z still laughs about the way Muhammad Ali welcomed him whenever their paths crossed.

The rapper laughed about it in Roc Nation’s roundtable for “The Greatest,” the Prime Video drama about Ali that Jay-Z helped bring to the screen.

The story came up when moderator Frazier Tharpe asked whether Jay-Z got to spend time with Ali.

“Yeah, for some reason he always wanted to punch me in the face,” Jay-Z joked, recalling how much he enjoyed the way Ali greeted him by putting a hand on his chin.

Long before those meetings, the boxer was a fixture on the television in Jay-Z’s childhood home in Brooklyn’s Marcy Houses.

“Ali was my first hero,” Jay-Z said as he described growing up in a household where music and sports were always on.

He said Ali taught him that having a public platform means accepting that people will disagree with you, telling Tharpe to “just do what you believe is right”; he also pointed to Ali’s example for younger people, saying fearlessness went hand in hand with hard work.

When the series needed someone to play the athlete Jay-Z grew up watching, the rapper paid attention to how Jaalen Best moved.

Jay-Z said Best’s footwork won him over and credited creator Ben Watkins with holding out for the right actor. Best said he auditioned about eight times over nearly 18 months and trained for nine months to play the boxer.

Best’s preparation covered a version of Ali who was still becoming the figure Jay-Z knew from TV.

Lonnie Ali, the boxer’s widow and one of the series’ executive producers, said the story follows him from his Olympic gold medal in Rome to his fight with Sonny Liston, including his family and upbringing in the segregated South.

Ali’s life outside the ring also shaped the series’ sound, which features a theme song from Wyclef Jean. The Fugees co-founder told AllHipHop he wanted to write a proper theme, and he made “Gladiator” with Watkins and singer Kofi Black.

All eight episodes premiered November 4 on Prime Video, where Michael Ealy plays Malcolm X opposite Best’s young Ali.
